title: Policy structure after the capacitated inventory continuous-order conjecture
short_statement: A four-period counterexample disproves a single connected ordering region under nonstationary demand. The remaining question is a useful exact structural description with a quantified number of reorder regions.
full_statement:
Fix a finite horizon $T$, integer inventory $x_t\in\mathbb Z$ (negative inventory denotes backorders), and a zero-lead-time integer order $q_t\in\{0,\ldots,B\}$ with fixed capacity $B\ge1$. Demands $D_t$ are independent, nonnegative, integer-valued, and have specified finite-support rational distributions that may vary by period. After ordering and demand, $x_{t+1}=x_t+q_t-D_t$. The cost is
$$K\mathbf1\{q_t>0\}+v q_t+h(x_{t+1})^++p(-x_{t+1})^+,$$
with $K,h,p>0$, $v\ge0$, and zero terminal cost. Minimize expected total cost over nonanticipative policies.

With $V_{T+1}=0$, the exact recursion is
$$V_t(x)=\min_{0\le q\le B}\left\{K\mathbf1\{q>0\}+vq+\mathbb E[h(x+q-D_t)^++p(D_t-x-q)^++V_{t+1}(x+q-D_t)]\right\}.$$
The minimum is over integer orders. Let $\mathcal O_t$ be the set of inventory levels at which every minimizing action orders a positive quantity. The continuous-order conjecture would make $\mathcal O_t$ a lower interval; this is false for nonstationary finite-horizon demand.

The remaining structural question is to bound and represent the number of separated ordering intervals and the associated order-up-to targets in terms of $T$, capacity, and demand support size, or prove that these can grow too rapidly for a uniformly small threshold description. Identify distributional assumptions restoring a simpler structure. Infinite-horizon iid demand and lost sales are separate variants: a finite-horizon backorder counterexample does not by itself settle their policy structure.
background: A fixed charge rewards batching, while a capacity limit prevents inventory from being restored in one large order. Their interaction can make ordering attractive at a higher inventory level but unattractive at a nearby lower one: paying the setup cost today changes how later constrained orders can be used. Consequently, ordinary convexity and a single reorder threshold are insufficient. The state is one-dimensional, so a useful structure theorem would improve both understanding and exact computation. This entry uses the finite-horizon backorder model of the cited counterexample rather than mixing several inventory models. It asks how complex an optimal rule must be after the simplest conjecture has failed.
open_problem: Bound the number and describe the structure of optimal ordering intervals and order-up-to targets in the stated finite-horizon capacitated backorder model, or exhibit families requiring unboundedly many intervals. Specify how complexity scales with horizon, capacity, and demand support; the continuous-order conjecture itself is already false.
known_results:
Rossi, Chen, and Tarim's paper appeared in European Journal of Operational Research 312(2):541-555 (2024), following its 2023 preprint. Conditional on the continuous-order property, it derives a modified multi-$(s,S)$ structure. Section 6, Example 3 and Tables 2-3, disprove that property with four independent nonstationary finite-support demands and $K=250$, $B=41$, $h=1$, $p=26$, $v=0$. In period 1, the displayed optimal action is zero at inventory 615, 41 at 616-618, and zero again at 619. This is a finite-horizon backorder result, not a stationary infinite-horizon or lost-sales counterexample.

Their numerical experiments support the usefulness of simple policies, but do not give a uniform approximation ratio or prove that every instance needs only a bounded number of thresholds.

Remaining open problem. Characterize the geometry and representational complexity of optimal reorder regions beyond the disproved continuous-order property, with the horizon and demand assumptions stated explicitly.

where_posed.text: Rossi, Chen, and Tarim discuss the longstanding structural question and disprove continuous ordering. The interval-complexity formulation is an editorial sharpening of the residual problem.

progress.summary: The continuous-order conjecture is disproved for finite-horizon nonstationary demand. The general exact structural-complexity question remains; the cited example does not resolve stationary infinite-horizon variants.

literature.synthesis: The earlier entry overstated the scope of the counterexample by placing it inside an infinite-horizon model and allowing lost sales. The published construction instead uses four periods, nonstationary independent demand, complete backorders, and zero lead time. Separating these cases leaves a concrete remaining target: quantify how complicated the reorder regions can become, rather than ask for an undefined 'simple' policy or repropose a conjecture already disproved. Observed rarity of violations is empirical evidence, not an approximation theorem.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Compute exact finite-horizon or discounted infinite-horizon policies for small integer-demand instances and classify the geometry of ordering regions. Search for invariants based on $K$-convexity variants, discrete convexity, or monotone comparative statics that survive the known counterexample.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: Match finite horizon, zero terminal cost, complete backorders, zero lead time, and independent but nonstationary demand. Use exact rational Bellman arithmetic for a finite counterexample. Explain why a finite state calculation covers all reachable states. An infinite-horizon counterexample needs its own stationary argument.
